question: What Is The Difference Between SOAP And REST?
answerGeneral: SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) is a protocol with strict standards: XML-only messages, a WSDL contract defining the service, built-in error handling (SOAP faults), and support for WS-Security and WS-AtomicTransaction. REST is an architectural style, not a protocol — it's lighter, uses any data format (usually JSON), leverages HTTP natively, and has no formal contract requirement. SOAP is still found in enterprise, banking, and government systems where strict contracts, transactional guarantees, and formal security are required. REST is dominant for web and mobile APIs because it's simpler, more flexible, and has a much smaller payload overhead.
answerGeneralTr: SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol), katı standartlara sahip bir protokoldür: yalnızca XML mesajları, hizmeti tanımlayan WSDL sözleşmesi, yerleşik hata işleme ve WS-Security desteği. REST ise bir mimari stildir, protokol değil — daha hafiftir, herhangi bir veri formatını kullanır (genellikle JSON), HTTP'den yerel olarak yararlanır ve resmi sözleşme gerektirmez. SOAP hâlâ katı sözleşmelerin, işlemsel garantilerin ve resmi güvenliğin gerekli olduğu kurumsal, bankacılık ve devlet sistemlerinde bulunmaktadır. REST ise daha basit, esnek ve çok daha az yük yüklü olduğu için web ve mobil API'ler için baskındır.

## SOAP vs REST

## Core Differences

```
                SOAP                    REST
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Type            Protocol                Architectural style
Format          XML only                Any (JSON, XML, CSV…)
Contract        WSDL (required)         OpenAPI (optional)
Transport       HTTP, SMTP, TCP…        HTTP only
Stateful        Can be                  Must be stateless
Security        WS-Security built-in    HTTPS + app-level auth
Error handling  SOAP Faults             HTTP status codes
Overhead        Heavy (XML envelope)    Lightweight (JSON body)
```

## A SOAP Request

```xml
POST /UserService HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: text/xml

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<soap:Envelope xmlns:soap="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/">
  <soap:Body>
    <GetUser xmlns="http://example.com/">
      <UserId>42</UserId>
    </GetUser>
  </soap:Body>
</soap:Envelope>
```

## The Equivalent REST Request

```
GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer token
```

## When SOAP Still Makes Sense

```
- Banking / financial transactions (ACID guarantees)
- Enterprise systems with existing SOAP infrastructure
- Formal contracts required between organisations
- WS-Security for signed/encrypted message envelopes
- Legacy system integration
```

question: What Are Query Parameters vs Path Parameters?
answerGeneral: Path parameters are part of the URL path and identify a specific resource: /users/42 — 42 is the path parameter identifying which user. They're required by definition (the URL doesn't exist without them). Query parameters come after the ? and are optional modifiers: /users?role=admin&sort=name — they filter, sort, paginate, or configure how a resource is returned. Rules of thumb: use path params for resource identity (what), use query params for filtering/sorting/pagination (how/which subset). Bad practice: /users/search?id=42 when /users/42 already exists.
answerGeneralTr: Path parametreleri URL yolunun bir parçasıdır ve belirli bir kaynağı tanımlar: /users/42 — 42, hangi kullanıcının olduğunu tanımlayan path parametresidir. Sorgu parametreleri, ? işaretinden sonra gelir ve isteğe bağlı değiştiricilerdir: /users?role=admin&sort=name — kaynağın nasıl döndürüleceğini filtreler, sıralar, sayfalar veya yapılandırır. Pratik kurallar: kaynak kimliği için path parametrelerini (ne), filtreleme/sıralama/sayfalama için sorgu parametrelerini (nasıl/hangi alt küme) kullanın.

## Path Parameters vs Query Parameters

## Path Parameters

```
/users/{userId}
/posts/{postId}/comments/{commentId}

✅ Identifies a specific resource
✅ Required — URL is incomplete without it
✅ Hierarchical — shows resource relationships

Examples:
GET /users/42              → User 42
GET /posts/10/comments/5   → Comment 5 on Post 10
GET /products/iphone-15    → Product by slug
```

## Query Parameters

```
/users?role=admin&sort=name&order=asc&page=2&limit=20

✅ Optional — resource exists without them
✅ Filtering, sorting, pagination, field selection
✅ Can have multiple values: ?tags=react&tags=typescript

Examples:
GET /products?category=phones&minPrice=500&inStock=true
GET /posts?author=42&status=published&sort=createdAt
GET /users?fields=id,name,email  (field selection)
```

## Common Mistakes

```typescript
// ❌ Action as path segment
GET /users/42/activate   → use PATCH instead
PATCH /users/42 { status: 'active' }  ✅

// ❌ Non-resource identity as path param
GET /search/react       → should be query param
GET /questions?topic=react  ✅

// ❌ Boolean filter as path segment
GET /products/available  → misleading hierarchy
GET /products?inStock=true  ✅

// ✅ Correct path vs query usage
GET /users/42           → Who is user 42?
GET /users?role=admin   → Which users are admins?
GET /users/42/posts     → Posts belonging to user 42
GET /users/42/posts?published=true → Filtered subset
```

question: How Do You Handle File Uploads In A REST API?
answerGeneral: File uploads can be handled two ways. Multipart form data (multipart/form-data) sends the file directly to your API endpoint alongside form fields — good for small files (under a few MB), simple to implement, but puts your API server in the hot path. Presigned URLs are the scalable approach: client requests a presigned upload URL from your API (which generates it using cloud SDK), client uploads directly to S3/GCS/Azure Blob (bypassing your server entirely), server receives a callback or the client sends back the file key. Benefits of presigned URLs: no bandwidth through your server, parallel uploads, client-side progress, leverages cloud storage infrastructure. Always validate file types, sizes, and scan for malware server-side.
answerGeneralTr: Dosya yüklemeleri iki şekilde ele alınabilir. Multipart form verisi (multipart/form-data) dosyayı form alanlarıyla birlikte doğrudan API endpoint'inize gönderir — küçük dosyalar için iyidir ancak API sunucunuzu kritik yola koyar. Ön imzalı URL'ler ölçeklenebilir yaklaşımdır: istemci API'nizden ön imzalı yükleme URL'si ister, istemci doğrudan S3/GCS/Azure Blob'a yükler (sunucunuzu tamamen atlayarak), sunucu bir geri arama alır. Ön imzalı URL'lerin faydaları: sunucunuzdan bant genişliği yok, paralel yüklemeler, istemci tarafı ilerleme. Her zaman dosya türlerini, boyutlarını doğrulayın ve sunucu tarafında kötü amaçlı yazılım taraması yapın.

question: What Is API Throttling And How Is It Different From Rate Limiting?
answerGeneral: Rate limiting and throttling are related but distinct. Rate limiting is a hard cap — once exceeded, requests are rejected with 429 until the window resets. Throttling is a softer control that slows requests down rather than rejecting them — it queues or delays excess requests to maintain a steady processing rate. Think of rate limiting as a bouncer turning people away, and throttling as a queue controlling how fast people enter. In practice the terms are often used interchangeably, but at scale: rate limiting protects against abuse, throttling manages fairness and quality of service across all users. Both are implemented to protect backend resources and ensure service stability.
answerGeneralTr: Hız sınırlama ve kısıtlama ilişkili ancak farklıdır. Hız sınırlama katı bir üst sınırdır — aşıldığında, pencere sıfırlanana kadar istekler 429 ile reddedilir. Kısıtlama daha yumuşak bir kontroldür — aşırı istekleri reddedmek yerine yavaşlatır. Hız sınırlamayı insanları geri çeviren bir güvenlik görevlisi, kısıtlamayı ise insanların ne kadar hızlı girdiğini kontrol eden bir kuyruk olarak düşünün. Pratikte terimler çoğunlukla birbirinin yerine kullanılır; ancak ölçekte: hız sınırlama kötüye kullanımdan korur, kısıtlama tüm kullanıcılarda adilliği ve hizmet kalitesini yönetir.
detailMd:
## Rate Limiting vs Throttling

## Rate Limiting — Hard Cap

```
100 requests/min limit:

Requests 1–100:    Processed normally  ✅
Request 101:       429 Too Many Requests ❌
Request 102–200:   All rejected until window resets ❌

Behaviour: Binary — allowed or rejected.
Response time: Immediate rejection.
UX: Client must wait and retry.
```

## Throttling — Controlled Rate

```
10 requests/sec throttle:

Burst of 50 requests arrives:
  First 10: Processed immediately  ✅
  Remaining 40: Queued, processed at 10/s  ⏳
  Total processing time: 5 seconds

Behaviour: Queued, not rejected.
Response time: Increased, not zero.
UX: Slower but eventually served.
```

## When To Use Each

```
Rate Limiting → External APIs, public endpoints
  Protect against abuse, bot scraping, runaway clients
  Clear boundary: exceed this and you're done

Throttling → Internal services, background jobs
  Ensure fair resource distribution
  Smooth out traffic spikes without losing requests
  Queue-based processing
```

## Combined Approach (Real Systems)

```
Free tier:  10 req/min rate limit + 2 req/s throttle
Pro tier:   500 req/min rate limit + 20 req/s throttle
Enterprise: Custom limits + SLA guarantees

Layer 1: Rate limiting at edge (Cloudflare / API Gateway)
Layer 2: Throttling at application level (queue depth)
Layer 3: Service protection (DB connection pool limits)
```

question: How Do You Validate API Request Bodies?
answerGeneral: Request validation ensures incoming data is safe, well-formed, and meets business rules before processing. Best practices: validate at the entry point (route handler), not deep in business logic; use a schema validation library (Zod, Joi, Yup) for declarative, composable rules; return detailed validation errors (field + message) so clients can display helpful UI; validate type, format, length, range, and required fields; sanitise strings to prevent injection. In Next.js with Zod: define a schema, parse the request body, return 422 with structured errors if invalid. Never trust the client — always validate even if you have frontend validation.
answerGeneralTr: İstek doğrulama, gelen verilerin işlenmeden önce güvenli, düzgün biçimlendirilmiş ve iş kurallarını karşıladığından emin olur. En iyi uygulamalar: iş mantığının derininde değil, giriş noktasında (route handler) doğrulayın; bildirimsel, birleştirilebilir kurallar için şema doğrulama kütüphanesi (Zod, Joi, Yup) kullanın; istemcilerin yardımcı UI gösterebilmesi için ayrıntılı doğrulama hataları döndürün (alan + mesaj); tür, format, uzunluk, aralık ve zorunlu alanları doğrulayın. Frontend doğrulamanız olsa bile asla istemciye güvenmeyin — her zaman doğrulayın.

question: What Is The Difference Between JWT And Session-Based Auth?
answerGeneral: Session-based auth stores session data on the server (in memory or a DB like Redis). The client receives a session ID cookie. On each request, the server looks up the session ID to get user data. JWTs (JSON Web Tokens) store user data client-side in a signed token. The server validates the signature on each request — no DB lookup needed. Comparison: sessions are stateful (easy to invalidate by deleting server-side), require shared storage in multi-server setups (Redis). JWTs are stateless (horizontally scalable, no shared storage needed), but can't be invalidated before expiry without a denylist. For most modern web apps, JWTs with short expiry (15min) and refresh tokens are the standard pattern.
answerGeneralTr: Oturum tabanlı kimlik doğrulama, oturum verilerini sunucuda depolar. İstemci bir oturum kimliği çerezi alır. Her istekte sunucu, kullanıcı verilerini almak için oturum kimliğini arar. JWT'ler, kullanıcı verilerini istemci tarafında imzalı bir token'da depolar. Sunucu her istekte imzayı doğrular — DB araması gerekmez. Oturumlar durum bilgilidir (sunucu tarafı silinerek kolayca geçersiz kılınabilir), çok sunuculu kurulumlarda paylaşılan depolama gerektirir. JWT'ler durum bilgisizdir (yatay olarak ölçeklenebilir), ancak bir denylist olmadan süresi dolmadan geçersiz kılınamaz.
detailMd:
## JWT vs Session-Based Auth

## Session-Based Flow

```
1. POST /login { email, password }
2. Server verifies credentials
3. Server creates session: sessions['abc123'] = { userId: 42, role: 'admin' }
4. Response: Set-Cookie: sessionId=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure
5. Subsequent requests: Cookie: sessionId=abc123
6. Server: lookup sessions['abc123'] → { userId: 42, role: 'admin' }

✅ Easy to invalidate (delete from sessions store)
✅ No user data in browser
❌ Requires shared session store (Redis) for multiple servers
❌ DB hit on every request
```

## JWT Flow

```
1. POST /login { email, password }
2. Server verifies credentials
3. Server signs: jwt.sign({ userId: 42, role: 'admin' }, SECRET, { expiresIn: '15m' })
4. Response: { accessToken: 'eyJ...', refreshToken: 'ryJ...' }
5. Subsequent requests: Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
6. Server: jwt.verify(token, SECRET) → payload (no DB hit)

✅ Stateless — horizontally scalable
✅ No shared storage needed
❌ Can't revoke before expiry (use short TTL + refresh tokens)
❌ Token lives in JS memory or localStorage (XSS risk)
```

## JWT Structure

```
eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9.eyJ1c2VySWQiOjQyfQ.signature
[    header (b64)    ].[    payload (b64)   ].[  sig   ]

Decode payload: { userId: 42, role: 'admin', iat: 1700000000, exp: 1700000900 }
⚠️ Payload is BASE64 ENCODED, not encrypted — don't put secrets in it!
```

## The Refresh Token Pattern

```
Access token:  15 min expiry — used for API calls
Refresh token: 7 days expiry — used only to get new access tokens

When access token expires:
  POST /auth/refresh { refreshToken }
  → new accessToken (+ optionally rotate refreshToken)

Log out: delete refresh token from DB/Redis → can no longer get new tokens
```

question: How Do You Document An API Effectively?
answerGeneral: Good API documentation is as important as the API itself — a poorly documented API won't get adopted. Key components: Overview (what the API does, base URL, auth method, versioning); Quick start (working example in under 5 minutes); Reference (every endpoint, all params, all request/response shapes, example values, error codes); Guides (common workflows, tutorials for key use cases); Changelog (what changed between versions). Best practices: auto-generate reference docs from OpenAPI spec to keep docs and code in sync; include copy-paste request examples in multiple languages (curl, JS, Python); document error codes, not just success cases; version the docs alongside the API. Tools: Swagger UI, Redoc, Stoplight, GitBook.
answerGeneralTr: İyi API belgeleri API kadar önemlidir — zayıf belgelenmiş bir API benimsenmez. Temel bileşenler: Genel Bakış (API'nin ne yaptığı, temel URL, kimlik doğrulama yöntemi, versiyonlama); Hızlı başlangıç (5 dakikadan kısa sürede çalışan örnek); Referans (her endpoint, tüm parametreler, tüm istek/yanıt şekilleri, örnek değerler, hata kodları); Kılavuzlar; Değişiklik günlüğü. En iyi uygulamalar: belgeleri ve kodu senkronize tutmak için OpenAPI spec'ten referans belgelerini otomatik oluşturun; birden fazla dilde kopyala-yapıştır istek örnekleri ekleyin; yalnızca başarı durumlarını değil hata kodlarını da belgeleyin.
detailMd:
## Effective API Documentation

## Structure of Great API Docs

```
1. Overview
   - What the API does in 2 sentences
   - Base URL: https://api.example.com/v1
   - Auth: Bearer token (how to obtain it)
   - Rate limits: 100 req/min

2. Quick Start (10-minute guide)
   - Minimal working example to get something useful
   - Real credentials / sandbox environment

3. Reference
   - Every endpoint: method, path, description
   - Request: headers, path params, query params, body schema
   - Response: schema with field descriptions
   - Error responses: all possible codes + meanings
   - Live examples with real-looking data

4. Guides & Tutorials
   - Common workflows (handle payment, upload file, webhook setup)
   - Code snippets in multiple languages

5. Changelog
   - Breaking changes clearly marked
   - Deprecation notices with migration paths
```

## Request Example (Multiple Languages)

```bash
# curl
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/questions \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"topic":"react","level":2,"question":"What is JSX?"}'
```

```typescript
// TypeScript
const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/v1/questions', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ topic: 'react', level: 2, question: 'What is JSX?' }),
});
const question = await response.json();
```

## Generating Docs From OpenAPI

```
openapi.yaml / openapi.json
    │
    ├── Swagger UI → Interactive docs (try endpoints live)
    ├── Redoc     → Clean read-only reference
    └── openapi-generator → Client SDKs (TypeScript, Python, Go)

Benefit: code is the source of truth → docs never go stale
```

question: What Is GraphQL Subscription And When Would You Use It?
answerGeneral: GraphQL Subscriptions provide real-time data by maintaining a persistent WebSocket connection between client and server. When subscribed data changes, the server pushes updates to connected clients. Useful for: live feeds (social media, stock prices), notifications, collaborative features (live cursors, shared documents), chat. Compared to polling: no wasted requests, instant updates. Compared to REST+WebSocket: subscriptions are typed and schema-driven, co-located with your other GraphQL operations. Trade-offs: WebSocket connections are stateful and consume server resources; at scale, you need a pub/sub broker (Redis) to propagate events across multiple server instances. Apollo Server, Yoga, and Hasura all support subscriptions.
answerGeneralTr: GraphQL Subscription'lar, istemci ve sunucu arasında kalıcı bir WebSocket bağlantısı sürdürerek gerçek zamanlı veri sağlar. Abone olunan veri değiştiğinde, sunucu bağlı istemcilere güncellemeler iter. Kullanım alanları: canlı akışlar (sosyal medya, hisse fiyatları), bildirimler, işbirlikçi özellikler, sohbet. Polling'e kıyasla: israf edilen istek yok, anlık güncellemeler. REST+WebSocket'e kıyasla: subscription'lar tiplendirilmiş ve şema odaklıdır. Dezavantajlar: WebSocket bağlantıları durumludur ve sunucu kaynakları tüketir; ölçekte, olayları birden fazla sunucu instance'ına yaymak için pub/sub aracısına ihtiyacınız var.

question: How Do You Handle API Security Beyond Authentication?
answerGeneral: Authentication is just the start — a comprehensive API security strategy covers: input validation (reject malformed/oversized payloads); SQL/NoSQL injection prevention (parameterised queries, ORMs); rate limiting and throttling (prevent abuse, brute force); CORS configuration (restrict origins); security headers (Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, Strict-Transport-Security); HTTPS only (no HTTP); sensitive data masking in logs; JWT best practices (short expiry, RS256 over HS256, validate audience/issuer); dependency scanning (npm audit); penetration testing; secrets management (never hardcode, use vaults); audit logging; principle of least privilege on DB and IAM permissions.
answerGeneralTr: Kimlik doğrulama yalnızca başlangıçtır — kapsamlı bir API güvenlik stratejisi şunları kapsar: giriş doğrulama; SQL/NoSQL enjeksiyonu önleme; hız sınırlama; CORS yapılandırması; güvenlik başlıkları; yalnızca HTTPS; günlüklerde hassas veri maskeleme; JWT en iyi uygulamaları; bağımlılık taraması; sızma testi; gizli yönetim; denetim günlükleme; DB ve IAM izinlerinde en az ayrıcalık ilkesi.

question: How Do You Design An API For Multiple Clients (Web, Mobile, Third-Party)?
answerGeneral: Serving multiple clients from one API requires careful design. Strategies: BFF pattern (one dedicated backend per client) for full independence; GraphQL with client-specified fields (web requests more, mobile requests less — same endpoint); API composition layer that aggregates microservices; versioned endpoints where different clients can adopt new versions at their pace. Key considerations: mobile has bandwidth/battery constraints (small payloads, avoid polling, use push notifications); web has more permissive requirements; third-party clients need stable contracts and long deprecation windows. Use feature flags to roll out API changes incrementally, monitoring client adoption before removing old fields.
answerGeneralTr: Birden fazla istemciye tek bir API'den hizmet vermek dikkatli tasarım gerektirir. Stratejiler: tam bağımsızlık için BFF deseni; istemcinin belirlediği alanlarla GraphQL; mikroservisleri toplayan API kompozisyon katmanı; farklı istemcilerin yeni sürümleri kendi hızlarında benimseyebildiği sürümlü endpoint'ler. Temel hususlar: mobil bant genişliği/pil kısıtlamalarına sahiptir (küçük yükler, polling'den kaçının, push bildirimleri kullanın); web daha esnek gereksinimlere sahiptir; üçüncü taraf istemciler kararlı sözleşmeler ve uzun kullanımdan kaldırma pencereleri ister.
detailMd:
## Multi-Client API Design

## The Core Tension

```
Web needs:    Full user profile, nested relationships, rich data
Mobile needs: Minimal payload (battery, bandwidth), push > polling
3rd Party:    Stable contract, versioned, well-documented, predictable

Single REST API serving all = inevitable compromises:
  - Too much data for mobile
  - Too little for web
  - Breaking changes affect all at once
```

## Strategy 1: GraphQL (Self-Describing Queries)

```graphql
# Web query — fetches everything needed
query DashboardData {
  user { name email role preferences { theme language } }
  recentOrders(first: 10) { id total status items { name } }
  notifications(unread: true) { id message createdAt }
}

# Mobile query — minimal payload
query MobileHome {
  user { name avatar }
  notifications(unread: true) { id }
}

# Same endpoint, different clients get exactly what they need
```

## Strategy 2: Response Field Selection

```
GET /users/42?fields=id,name,avatar     → Mobile (small)
GET /users/42                           → Web (full response)
GET /users/42?expand[]=orders           → Third-party (explicit expand)
```

## Strategy 3: BFF Per Client

```
/api/web/*    → Web BFF: orchestrates, returns rich payloads
/api/mobile/* → Mobile BFF: returns compact, push-optimised responses
/api/v1/*     → Public API: versioned, stable, rate-limited
```

## Client-Specific Considerations

```
Mobile:
  ✓ gzip/brotli compression
  ✓ Conditional requests (ETag) to avoid re-downloading unchanged data
  ✓ Push notifications (FCM/APNs) instead of polling
  ✓ Offline-first: return stale data + background sync

Third-Party:
  ✓ Semantic versioning for the API
  ✓ 6–12 month deprecation windows
  ✓ Sandbox environment with test credentials
  ✓ Webhook support for event-driven integration
  ✓ SDKs in popular languages
```

question: What Is Event-Driven Architecture And How Does It Relate To APIs?
answerGeneral: Event-driven architecture (EDA) is a design pattern where services communicate by producing and consuming events (facts about things that happened) rather than making direct API calls to each other. Instead of Service A calling Service B synchronously, A publishes an 'OrderPlaced' event to a message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, AWS SNS/SQS), and B subscribes and processes it independently. This decouples services: A doesn't need to know B exists; B can be added, changed, or fail without affecting A. APIs and EDA coexist: REST/GraphQL APIs remain the external synchronous interface; EDA handles internal service-to-service communication. Challenges: eventual consistency, complex debugging, event schema versioning, ordering guarantees.
answerGeneralTr: Olay odaklı mimari (EDA), servislerin birbirine doğrudan API çağrısı yapmak yerine olay üreterek ve tüketerek iletişim kurduğu bir tasarım modelidir. Servis A, Servis B'yi doğrudan çağırmak yerine bir mesaj aracısına 'OrderPlaced' olayı yayınlar ve B bağımsız olarak abone olup işler. Bu, servisleri ayırır: A, B'nin var olduğunu bilmek zorunda değildir. API'ler ve EDA bir arada bulunur: REST/GraphQL API'ler harici senkron arayüz olmaya devam eder; EDA dahili servis-servis iletişimini ele alır. Zorluklar: nihai tutarlılık, karmaşık hata ayıklama, olay şeması versiyonlaması.
detailMd:
## Event-Driven Architecture

## Request-Driven vs Event-Driven

```
Request-Driven (REST calls)
  Order Service → [POST /inventory/reserve] → Inventory Service
  Order Service → [POST /emails/send]       → Email Service
  Order Service → [POST /payments/charge]   → Payment Service

  Problems: Tight coupling, cascade failures, synchronous blocking

Event-Driven
  Order Service → [OrderPlaced event] → Message Broker
                                            │
              ┌─────────────────────────────┤
              ▼             ▼               ▼
  Inventory Service  Email Service  Payment Service
  (subscribe & process independently)

  Benefits: Loose coupling, independent scaling, fault isolation
```

## Event Schema Design

```typescript
// Events should be past-tense facts, include all needed context
interface OrderPlacedEvent {
  eventId: string;       // for idempotency
  eventType: 'order.placed';
  version: '1.0';
  timestamp: string;     // ISO 8601
  payload: {
    orderId: string;
    customerId: string;
    items: { productId: string; quantity: number; price: number }[];
    total: number;
    currency: 'GBP' | 'USD' | 'EUR';
  };
}
```

## Event Versioning

```
Challenge: consumers may not update at the same time as producers

Strategies:
  1. Additive only — add fields, never remove (same as REST)
  2. Version in event type: 'order.placed.v2'
  3. Schema registry (Confluent) — producers and consumers
     validate against registered schema
```

## Outbox Pattern (Reliability)

```
Problem: writing to DB + publishing event = two separate operations
         If app crashes between them, event is lost

Solution: Outbox pattern
  1. Write order to DB + write event to outbox table (same transaction)
  2. Background worker reads outbox and publishes to broker
  3. Delete from outbox after confirmed publish
  = At-least-once delivery with exactly-once semantics via idempotency
```
